newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China to send HK reinforcements before handover.
newsitem.headline: China to send HK reinforcements before handover.

text.p: Britain caved in on Monday to Chinese demands to send 500 extra troops into Hong Kong just before British rule ends next week.
Almost 200 People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops have already arrived in Hong Kong for the June 30 handover and Britain had resisted any more coming in.

China's Xinhua news agency announced from Beijing that Britain had agreed after protracted negotiations that 509 PLA troops and 39 vehicles would now enter Hong Kong on the evening of the handover at 9.00 p.m. (1300 GMT).

"The purpose of the agreement concluded by the two sides is to ensure that the PLA be able to perform its defence duties in Hong Kong from zero hour of July 1," Xinhua quoted an unidentified Chinese official as saying.
As the stock market waxed and British rule waned, Hong Kong's last governor Chris Patten said on Monday the territory was like a Rolls-Royce limousine and China should not tinker with it.

In the final week before communist China takes rampantly capitalist Hong Kong back, the Hang Seng Index hit a new record high, top executives exuded business confidence and democratic activists kept up the pressure for political freedom.
After 150 years of what it sees as imperialist humiliation, China views Hong Kong's laissez-faire economy as the jewel in its communist crown. But Patten urged a light touch.
"When you have a Rolls-Royce, there is no need to spend a lot of time tinkering around with the engine," Britain's 28th colonial governor told a business conference.

"I think this community has done enough to be trusted and to be allowed to get on with its life," he said of the world's seventh largest trading economy, which is being granted 50 years of autonomy under a "one country, two systems" formula.
Patten urged his successor, 60-year-old shipping billionaire Tung Chee-hwa, not to be an autocrat.

"In Hong Kong, there is no one who has absolute power," he told the Chinese-language paper Ming Pao in an interview marking the end of British rule in a colony that has boasted growth of up to six percent a year over the past decade.
The temperature rose and fell sharply on the Hang Seng Index, barometer of business confidence in this capitalist enclave facing an uncertain future under communist rule.

The market, which made its biggest ever one-day gain on Friday, jumped by more than one percent to a new high of 15,322.33 before profit-takers wiped off the gains. It finally closed 133 points down at 15,021 after a seesaw day.

An overwhelming 92 percent of executives polled at a Far Eastern Economic Review conference said they were positive. The survey showed that maintaining a democratic system was ranked as the least important factor for Hong Kong's economic well-being.

But Democracy leader Martin Lee, attacked by Tung for "bad-mouthing" Hong Kong around the world, kept up the pressure on China now the eyes of the world are focused on the run-up to the June 30 handover.
Lee denounced the unelected provisional legislature set up by Beijing as a threat to Hong Kong's future.
"Why should the legislature give us good laws if they have not even been elected?" he demanded. "We cannot expect judges to protect us if the laws are bad."
A century after Queen Empress Victoria celebrated her golden jubilee, the royal yacht Britannia sailed into Hong Kong to end the colonial era with an elegant flourish.
The ship is to be temporary home to Prince Charles, who used to play on its decks as a child and took Princess Diana on board for the honeymoon start to his ill-fated marriage.
In an emotional farewell rich in imperial symbolism, the heir to the throne will sail off into the imperial sunset after handing over to China this once insignificant rock.
